BYD looking to build 5-minute EV charging network in Canada

A Toronto-based job posting from the Chinese automaker revealed it's looking into a flash-charging network in this country

Last updated Jun 15, 2026

You can save this article by registering for free here. Or sign-in if you have an account.

  • China’s BYD may be looking to build a flash-charging network in Canada, to top up EVs in five minutes
  • Flash-chargers provide more than three times the power of any public chargers in North America
  • BYD has built nearly 6,000 flash-chargers in China in last 12 months, and recently its first in the U.K.

Oh, what a job posting reveals. Chinese automaker BYD has posted a Toronto-based job for a manager to set up and oversee “BYD’s flash-charging network expansion strategy and business growth across Canada.” The megawatt-power chargers in that network would reportedly each be able to add approximately 400 kilometres of range to an EV’s battery in just five minutes.

Of course, as with all things Chinese-EV-related, there is a caveat. To achieve such rapid charging, the megawatt charger needs to be plugged into a BYD electric vehicle outfitted with either the 1,000-volt Super e-Platform; or the new second-generation Blade battery, which boasts a whopping 1,500-kilowatt charging capacity. Impressive when you consider that Tesla’s new V4 Superchargers max out at 500 kW, and most North American EVs can only take, at the max, 350 kW.

Electrek reports that there are currently nearly 6,000 flash-chargers up and running in China, and that robust network is deploying 2.4 times more charging power per month than Tesla adds to its Supercharger network. These chargers provide more than three times the power output of any public chargers in North America. BYD has set a goal of 20,000 flash chargers in China by the end of the year.

With BYD – an acronym for “Build Your Dream” – tipping its hand with this new Flash Charging Business Development Manager job posting, it’s only logical the automaker’d aim to bring its electric vehicles to Canada, too. Does it follow that since the annual number of EVs allowed into Canada with the low six-per-cent tariff is capped at just 49,000, split between not only Chinese brands but Tesla, Volvo, and Polestar, that BYD has designs of assembling or even building its advanced all-electrics in Canada? Establishing a flash-charging network is a costly undertaking, and one you’d figure justified only if the end game is for a large number of BYD vehicles to use it.

It should be noted BYD has posted openings for more than 10 management jobs across its Canadian launch team; and as we reported recently, BYD is actively seeking sites for 20 dealerships across the country.

The flash-charging manager job calls for five years of experience in public charging networks or energy storage. Here’s the list of responsibilities: building cost and profit models for flash-charging in Canada, including subsidy policies; developing local partners for power-grid upgrades, equipment installation, and on-site operation services; formulating a reasonable network plan for flash-charging stations; managing station construction projects in coordination with BYD headquarters; and jointly operating the stations with local partners.

This is massive news for Canada’s public charger network, as if and when these flash-chargers open for business, the country will have a much more robust charging than the United States. Also, with one of the knocks against operating EVs in Canada being the cold climate in many provinces, this kind of fast-charging makes operation in winter more palatable. BYD claims its new Blade battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes at -20°C (-4°F).

One of the challenges the new flash-charging manager will face is the layers of bureaucracy involved in permitting and building public charging stations. Those aforementioned 5,700 flash-chargers were built in China in the past 12 months, so it will be interesting to see how long it will take for BYD to build and open the first 100 in Canada.

BYD looking to build 5-minute EV charging network in Canada

A Toronto-based job posting from the Chinese automaker revealed it's looking into a flash-charging network in this country

Last updated Jun 15, 2026

You can save this article by registering for free here. Or sign-in if you have an account.

  • China’s BYD may be looking to build a flash-charging network in Canada, to top up EVs in five minutes
  • Flash-chargers provide more than three times the power of any public chargers in North America
  • BYD has built nearly 6,000 flash-chargers in China in last 12 months, and recently its first in the U.K.

Oh, what a job posting reveals. Chinese automaker BYD has posted a Toronto-based job for a manager to set up and oversee “BYD’s flash-charging network expansion strategy and business growth across Canada.” The megawatt-power chargers in that network would reportedly each be able to add approximately 400 kilometres of range to an EV’s battery in just five minutes.

Of course, as with all things Chinese-EV-related, there is a caveat. To achieve such rapid charging, the megawatt charger needs to be plugged into a BYD electric vehicle outfitted with either the 1,000-volt Super e-Platform; or the new second-generation Blade battery, which boasts a whopping 1,500-kilowatt charging capacity. Impressive when you consider that Tesla’s new V4 Superchargers max out at 500 kW, and most North American EVs can only take, at the max, 350 kW.

Electrek reports that there are currently nearly 6,000 flash-chargers up and running in China, and that robust network is deploying 2.4 times more charging power per month than Tesla adds to its Supercharger network. These chargers provide more than three times the power output of any public chargers in North America. BYD has set a goal of 20,000 flash chargers in China by the end of the year.

With BYD – an acronym for “Build Your Dream” – tipping its hand with this new Flash Charging Business Development Manager job posting, it’s only logical the automaker’d aim to bring its electric vehicles to Canada, too. Does it follow that since the annual number of EVs allowed into Canada with the low six-per-cent tariff is capped at just 49,000, split between not only Chinese brands but Tesla, Volvo, and Polestar, that BYD has designs of assembling or even building its advanced all-electrics in Canada? Establishing a flash-charging network is a costly undertaking, and one you’d figure justified only if the end game is for a large number of BYD vehicles to use it.

It should be noted BYD has posted openings for more than 10 management jobs across its Canadian launch team; and as we reported recently, BYD is actively seeking sites for 20 dealerships across the country.

The flash-charging manager job calls for five years of experience in public charging networks or energy storage. Here’s the list of responsibilities: building cost and profit models for flash-charging in Canada, including subsidy policies; developing local partners for power-grid upgrades, equipment installation, and on-site operation services; formulating a reasonable network plan for flash-charging stations; managing station construction projects in coordination with BYD headquarters; and jointly operating the stations with local partners.

This is massive news for Canada’s public charger network, as if and when these flash-chargers open for business, the country will have a much more robust charging than the United States. Also, with one of the knocks against operating EVs in Canada being the cold climate in many provinces, this kind of fast-charging makes operation in winter more palatable. BYD claims its new Blade battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes at -20°C (-4°F).

One of the challenges the new flash-charging manager will face is the layers of bureaucracy involved in permitting and building public charging stations. Those aforementioned 5,700 flash-chargers were built in China in the past 12 months, so it will be interesting to see how long it will take for BYD to build and open the first 100 in Canada.
